claim: The climbing fiber input to Purkinje cells acts as a teaching signal by triggering a massive influx of dendritic calcium that marks the occurrence of instructive stimuli during cerebellar learning.
source: The climbing fiber input to Purkinje cells acts as a teaching signal by triggering a massive influx of dendritic calcium that marks the occurrence of instructive stimuli during cerebellar learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established scientific understanding about climbing fiber function in cerebellar learning.

claim: Information about airpuff duration and pressure was encoded probabilistically across repeated trials in Purkinje cell dendrites.
source: Information about airpuff duration and pressure was encoded probabilistically across repeated trials, and in two additional signals in single trials: the synchrony of calcium spikes in the Purkinje cell population, and the amplitude of the calcium spikes, which was modulated by a non-climbing fiber pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing how calcium events vary with stimulus parameters.

claim: The synchrony of calcium spikes in the Purkinje cell population encodes information about airpuff strength in single trials.
source: Information about airpuff duration and pressure was encoded probabilistically across repeated trials, and in two additional signals in single trials: the synchrony of calcium spikes in the Purkinje cell population, and the amplitude of the calcium spikes, which was modulated by a non-climbing fiber pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of population synchrony shown in the results.

claim: The amplitude of calcium spikes in Purkinje cells is modulated by a non-climbing fiber pathway.
source: Information about airpuff duration and pressure was encoded probabilistically across repeated trials, and in two additional signals in single trials: the synchrony of calcium spikes in the Purkinje cell population, and the amplitude of the calcium spikes, which was modulated by a non-climbing fiber pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-CF signals that modulate calcium event amplitude.

claim: Calcium-based teaching signals in Purkinje cells contain analog information that encodes the strength of instructive stimuli trial-by-trial.
source: These results indicate that calcium-based teaching signals in Purkinje cells contain analog information that encodes the strength of instructive stimuli trial-by-trial.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The climbing fiber input to Purkinje cells plays a key role in theories of cerebellar learning by providing a teaching signal.
source: The climbing fiber (CF) input to Purkinje cells (PCs) plays a key role in theories of cerebellar learning (Houk et al., 1996; Ito, 2000) by providing a teaching signal that sounds the alarm when an unexpected sensory event is encountered (Simpson et al., 1996; De Zeeuw et al., 1998; Ito, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established theories in the field.

claim: Some climbing fibers fire a burst of spikes when an unexpected periocular airpuff is delivered.
source: Previous work has shown that some CFs fire a burst of spikes when the unexpected periocular airpuff is delivered (Sears and Steinmetz, 1991; Nicholson and Freeman, 2003), and that this signal is sufficient for conditioning (Mauk et al., 1986; Thompson et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The climbing fiber signal is sufficient for eyeblink conditioning.
source: Previous work has shown that some CFs fire a burst of spikes when the unexpected periocular airpuff is delivered (Sears and Steinmetz, 1991; Nicholson and Freeman, 2003), and that this signal is sufficient for conditioning (Mauk et al., 1986; Thompson et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: The strength of the periocular airpuff has a major impact on the magnitude and rate of learning.
source: However, we do not understand how CF signals encode even the most basic stimulus features such as the strength of the periocular airpuff, which has a major impact on the magnitude and the rate of learning (Spence, 1953; Smith, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Climbing fibers fire bursts spontaneously at approximately 1 Hz.
source: CFs fire bursts spontaneously at ∼1 Hz (Thach, 1968), a low rate that is barely modulated during sensory stimulation (Simpson et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The spontaneous firing rate of climbing fibers is barely modulated during sensory stimulation.
source: CFs fire bursts spontaneously at ∼1 Hz (Thach, 1968), a low rate that is barely modulated during sensory stimulation (Simpson et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Climbing fibers are often described as binary because they respond by either not firing at all or firing a single burst regardless of stimulus strength.
source: Indeed, CFs are often described as binary because they respond by either not firing at all or firing a single burst regardless of how strongly they are stimulated (Crill, 1970; Gibson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous characterizations of CF responses.

claim: In the adult cerebellum, each Purkinje cell is innervated by only one climbing fiber.
source: Another peculiarity is that in the adult cerebellum, each PC is innervated by only one CF (Simpson et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The climbing fiber-Purkinje cell synapse is one of the most powerful and reliable synapses in the brain.
source: The CF-PC synapse is one of the most powerful and reliable in the brain (Schmolesky et al., 2002; Ohtsuki et al., 2009): each time the CF fires a burst, it evokes in PCs both a burst of sodium spikes in the soma known as a complex spike (Eccles et al., 1966; Thach, 1968), and a massive calcium-based spike in the dendrite (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous physiological studies.

claim: Each time a climbing fiber fires a burst, it evokes a complex spike in the Purkinje cell soma.
source: The CF-PC synapse is one of the most powerful and reliable in the brain (Schmolesky et al., 2002; Ohtsuki et al., 2009): each time the CF fires a burst, it evokes in PCs both a burst of sodium spikes in the soma known as a complex spike (Eccles et al., 1966; Thach, 1968), and a massive calcium-based spike in the dendrite (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classic electrophysiological studies.

claim: Each time a climbing fiber fires a burst, it evokes a massive calcium-based spike in the Purkinje cell dendrite.
source: The CF-PC synapse is one of the most powerful and reliable in the brain (Schmolesky et al., 2002; Ohtsuki et al., 2009): each time the CF fires a burst, it evokes in PCs both a burst of sodium spikes in the soma known as a complex spike (Eccles et al., 1966; Thach, 1968), and a massive calcium-based spike in the dendrite (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous calcium imaging studies.

claim: Analog information may be encoded probabilistically in the total number of bursts generated by an individual climbing fiber across many repeated presentations of the same stimulus.
source: Based on these observations, it has been suggested that analog information may be encoded probabilistically, in the total number of bursts generated by an individual CF across many repeated presentations of the same stimulus (Fujita, 1982; Kenyon et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical proposals.

claim: Sensory events synchronize climbing fibers.
source: Others have pointed out that sensory events synchronize CFs (Llinás and Sasaki, 1989; Lou and Bloedel, 1992; Wylie et al., 1995; Ozden et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2009; Wise et al., 2010), which raises the possibility that stimulus information may be available in the precise timing of CF inputs (Schweighofer et al., 2004; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008), or in the level of co-activation in the CF population (Ghosh et al., 2011; Tokuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental observations.

claim: Stimulus information may be available in the precise timing of climbing fiber inputs.
source: Others have pointed out that sensory events synchronize CFs (Llinás and Sasaki, 1989; Lou and Bloedel, 1992; Wylie et al., 1995; Ozden et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2009; Wise et al., 2010), which raises the possibility that stimulus information may be available in the precise timing of CF inputs (Schweighofer et al., 2004; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008), or in the level of co-activation in the CF population (Ghosh et al., 2011; Tokuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: Stimulus information may be available in the level of co-activation in the climbing fiber population.
source: Others have pointed out that sensory events synchronize CFs (Llinás and Sasaki, 1989; Lou and Bloedel, 1992; Wylie et al., 1995; Ozden et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2009; Wise et al., 2010), which raises the possibility that stimulus information may be available in the precise timing of CF inputs (Schweighofer et al., 2004; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008), or in the level of co-activation in the CF population (Ghosh et al., 2011; Tokuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: Analog information about instructive stimulus strength might be encoded post-synaptically by modulating the size of the Purkinje cell response to individual sensory-driven climbing fiber bursts.
source: Recent findings suggest an additional possibility: analog information, like the strength of an instructive stimulus, might be encoded post-synaptically by modulating the size of the PC response to individual sensory-driven CF bursts (Maruta et al., 2007; Najafi et al., 2014; Yang and Lisberger, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent experimental findings.

claim: Purkinje cell dendrites in the experiments appeared as parasagittally aligned, tube-like structures.
source: As in previous reports (Sullivan et al., 2005; Ozden et al., 2008), PC dendrites in our experiments appeared as parasagittally aligned, tube-like structures (Figure 1A), in which large calcium transients (Figure 1B, circles) occurred spontaneously and in response to periocular airpuff stimuli (Figure 1B, triangles).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations and Figure 1A, as well as citations to previous reports.

claim: Large calcium transients occurred spontaneously and in response to periocular airpuff stimuli in Purkinje cell dendrites.
source: As in previous reports (Sullivan et al., 2005; Ozden et al., 2008), PC dendrites in our experiments appeared as parasagittally aligned, tube-like structures (Figure 1A), in which large calcium transients (Figure 1B, circles) occurred spontaneously and in response to periocular airpuff stimuli (Figure 1B, triangles).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Calcium transients in Purkinje cell dendrites are triggered by activation of the climbing fiber input.
source: We have previously shown that these calcium transients are triggered in each individual PC dendrite by activation of its one-and-only climbing fiber (CF) input, which also evokes a complex spike in the PC somata (Ozden et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Spontaneous calcium events occurred at about 1 Hz (0.4–1.4 Hz; median 0.7 Hz).
source: First, they occurred spontaneously at about 1 Hz (0.4–1.4 Hz; median 0.7 Hz; Figure 1C), which is similar to the characteristic spontaneous firing rate of CFs reported previously in awake animals (Thach, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The spontaneous calcium event frequency is similar to the characteristic spontaneous firing rate of climbing fibers reported previously in awake animals.
source: First, they occurred spontaneously at about 1 Hz (0.4–1.4 Hz; median 0.7 Hz; Figure 1C), which is similar to the characteristic spontaneous firing rate of CFs reported previously in awake animals (Thach, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited previous work.

claim: Calcium events had a fast rise of approximately 10 ms.
source: Second, they had a fast rise (∼10 ms Figure 1D), as observed for CF-triggered signals in other calcium imaging studies (Miyakawa et al., 1992; Eilers et al., 1995; Schmidt et al., 2003), and a slower decay t1/2 of 74 ± 13 ms (mean ± SD), which is in the midrange of previously observed kinetics using synthetic indicators (decay t1/2 = 25–170 ms; [Sullivan et al., 2005; Sarkisov and Wang, 2008; Ozden et al., 2009; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Calcium events had a slower decay t1/2 of 74 ± 13 ms (mean ± SD).
source: Second, they had a fast rise (∼10 ms Figure 1D), as observed for CF-triggered signals in other calcium imaging studies (Miyakawa et al., 1992; Eilers et al., 1995; Schmidt et al., 2003), and a slower decay t1/2 of 74 ± 13 ms (mean ± SD), which is in the midrange of previously observed kinetics using synthetic indicators (decay t1/2 = 25–170 ms; [Sullivan et al., 2005; Sarkisov and Wang, 2008; Ozden et al., 2009; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The decay kinetics of calcium events is in the midrange of previously observed kinetics using synthetic indicators (decay t1/2 = 25–170 ms).
source: Second, they had a fast rise (∼10 ms Figure 1D), as observed for CF-triggered signals in other calcium imaging studies (Miyakawa et al., 1992; Eilers et al., 1995; Schmidt et al., 2003), and a slower decay t1/2 of 74 ± 13 ms (mean ± SD), which is in the midrange of previously observed kinetics using synthetic indicators (decay t1/2 = 25–170 ms; [Sullivan et al., 2005; Sarkisov and Wang, 2008; Ozden et al., 2009; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011]).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited previous studies.

claim: The probability of observing two spontaneous calcium events at the same time was highest for adjacent Purkinje cell dendrites.
source: Third, the probability of observing two spontaneous calcium events at the same time was highest for adjacent PC dendrites, and decreased rapidly as the mediolateral distance between dendrites increased (Figure 1E, black).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The probability of observing two spontaneous calcium events at the same time decreased rapidly as the mediolateral distance between dendrites increased.
source: Third, the probability of observing two spontaneous calcium events at the same time was highest for adjacent PC dendrites, and decreased rapidly as the mediolateral distance between dendrites increased (Figure 1E, black).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The spatial pattern of spontaneous calcium event synchrony is consistent with previous studies demonstrating the prevalence of synchronous climbing fiber input to neighboring Purkinje cells in the same parasagittal microzone.
source: This finding is consistent with previous studies demonstrating the prevalence of synchronous CF input to neighboring PCs in the same parasagittal microzone (Bell and Kawasaki, 1972; Sasaki et al., 1989; Ozden et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited previous studies.

claim: 101 sites on the surface of cerebellar cortex were imaged in 22 mice.
source: We imaged 101 sites on the surface of cerebellar cortex in 22 mice, including paravermal locations in lobules V, VI, and more lateral locations in simplex (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is a direct statement of the experimental methods and sample size.

claim: Imaging sites included paravermal locations in lobules V, VI, and more lateral locations in simplex.
source: We imaged 101 sites on the surface of cerebellar cortex in 22 mice, including paravermal locations in lobules V, VI, and more lateral locations in simplex (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental description and Figure 2A,B.

claim: Many dendrites in the paravermal regions of lobules V and VI responded to periocular airpuff stimulation with a climbing fiber-triggered calcium event.
source: Consistent with the location of trigeminal CFs reported in previous studies (Miles and Wiesendanger, 1975a, 1975b; Manni and Petrosini, 2004), we found that many dendrites in the paravermal regions of lobules V and VI responded to periocular airpuff stimulation with a CF-triggered calcium event (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D and citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Dendrites on the surface of lobule simplex were mostly unresponsive to periocular airpuff stimulation.
source: In contrast, dendrites on the surface of lobule simplex were mostly unresponsive, which is expected given the deep location of periocularly-related CF zones in this lobule (Hesslow, 1994; Mostofi et al., 2010; Heiney et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Some dendrites responded with a climbing fiber-triggered calcium event only after ipsilateral periocular airpuffs.
source: As observed in electrophysiological work (Hesslow, 1994; Mostofi et al., 2010), we found two types of periocular PC dendrites that could be classified according to the receptive field properties of their CF inputs: some dendrites responded with a CF-triggered calcium event only after ipsilateral periocular airpuffs (Figure 2B,C), while others had bilateral CF receptive fields and responded after ipsi- and contralateral periocular airpuffs (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C and citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: Some dendrites had bilateral climbing fiber receptive fields and responded after ipsi- and contralateral periocular airpuffs.
source: As observed in electrophysiological work (Hesslow, 1994; Mostofi et al., 2010), we found two types of periocular PC dendrites that could be classified according to the receptive field properties of their CF inputs: some dendrites responded with a CF-triggered calcium event only after ipsilateral periocular airpuffs (Figure 2B,C), while others had bilateral CF receptive fields and responded after ipsi- and contralateral periocular airpuffs (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,D and citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The likelihood of eliciting a response in an individual climbing fiber is proportional to stimulus intensity.
source: Previous studies indicate that the likelihood of eliciting a response in an individual CF is proportional to stimulus intensity (Eccles et al., 1972b; Bosman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Climbing fiber-triggered calcium events occurred more reliably as the duration of the airpuff was increased.
source: The raster plots of all the PC dendrites in our entire duration dataset demonstrate that CF-triggered calcium events occurred more reliably as the duration of the airpuff was increased (Figure 3A bottom; top: average).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The probability of calcium events increased gradually with increasing airpuff duration (two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 238.5, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.01 for all pairwise comparisons).
source: On average across all the PC dendrites, we found that the probability of calcium events increased gradually with increasing airpuff duration (Figure 3B, left; two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 238.5, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.01 for all pairwise comparisons), and pressure (Figure 3B, right; two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 58.93, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.001 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The probability of calcium events increased gradually with increasing airpuff pressure (two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 58.93, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.001 for all pairwise comparisons).
source: On average across all the PC dendrites, we found that the probability of calcium events increased gradually with increasing airpuff duration (Figure 3B, left; two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 238.5, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.01 for all pairwise comparisons), and pressure (Figure 3B, right; two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 58.93, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.001 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 58% of individual dendrites showed graded increase of calcium event probability with airpuff duration.
source: The graded increase of calcium event probability with airpuff duration, which is shown averaged across all dendrites in Figure 3B, was evident in 58% of the individual dendrites (Figure 3C, top row), in which the probability and the stimulus duration increased with the same rank order.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of individual dendrite data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 42% of dendrites were relatively unresponsive to all airpuffs below a certain threshold and responded with similar probability for all durations higher than the threshold.
source: The remaining 42% of the dendrites were relatively unresponsive to all airpuffs below a certain threshold (Figure 3C, arrowheads), and responded with similar probability for all durations higher than the threshold (Figure 3C, rows 2–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of individual dendrite data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The response probability of individual climbing fibers showed monotonic (non-decreasing) dependence on stimulus duration, with a dependency that ranged from graded to threshold-like.
source: In summary, the response probability of individual CFs showed monotonic (i.e., non-decreasing) dependence on stimulus duration, with a dependency that ranged from graded to threshold-like.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Calcium events were evoked in Purkinje cell dendrites at a wide range of latencies relative to the onset of the airpuff stimulus (onset latency: approximately 25–150 ms).
source: In agreement with previous electrophysiological reports of sensory-driven CFs (Ekerot et al., 1987; Kobayashi et al., 1998), we found that calcium events were evoked in PC dendrites at a wide range of latencies relative to the onset of the airpuff stimulus (onset latency: ∼25–150 ms; Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Increasing the duration of the periocular airpuff resulted in progressively more long-latency calcium events (67.1 ± 1.5, 71.8 ± 1.8, 78.8 ± 1.4, and 80.9 ± 1.4 ms for d1–d4 respectively; two-way ANOVA: F[393] = 11.85, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d1–d2 comparison and d3–d4 comparison).
source: Increasing the duration of the periocular airpuff resulted in progressively more long-latency calcium events (Figure 4A–C left; 67.1 ± 1.5, 71.8 ± 1.8, 78.8 ± 1.4, and 80.9 ± 1.4 ms for d1–d4 respectively; two-way ANOVA: F[393] = 11.85, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d1–d2 comparison and d3–d4 comparison).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The temporal jitter of calcium events was reduced with increasing airpuff duration (23.3 ± 1.2, 21.1 ± 1.0, 19.3 ± 0.7, and 18.0 ± 0.8 ms for d1–d4 respectively; two-way ANOVA: F[393] = 5.42, p < 0.01; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 for d1–d3, d1–d4, d2–d4 comparisons).
source: The temporal jitter, as quantified by median absolute deviation from median latency (Figure 4C, right), was also reduced (23.3 ± 1.2, 21.1 ± 1.0, 19.3 ± 0.7, and 18.0 ± 0.8 ms for d1–d4 respectively; two-way ANOVA: F[393] = 5.42, p < 0.01; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 for d1–d3, d1–d4, d2–d4 comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Long-duration airpuffs evoked significantly more calcium events than short-duration airpuffs in the interval 75–150 ms after periocular stimulation (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p < 0.0001).
source: The analysis shown in Figure 4B confirmed that long-duration airpuffs evoked significantly more calcium events than short-duration airpuffs in the interval 75–150 ms after the periocular stimulation (Figure 4B; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p < 0.0001) but not in the interval 0–75 ms (Figure 4B; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p = 0.8).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Long-duration airpuffs did not evoke significantly more calcium events than short-duration airpuffs in the interval 0–75 ms after periocular stimulation (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p = 0.8).
source: The analysis shown in Figure 4B confirmed that long-duration airpuffs evoked significantly more calcium events than short-duration airpuffs in the interval 75–150 ms after the periocular stimulation (Figure 4B; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p < 0.0001) but not in the interval 0–75 ms (Figure 4B; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p = 0.8).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Varying airpuff pressure led to a modest reduction in onset latency (81.3 ± 2.4 vs 79.6 ± 3.4 ms for p1 and p2 respectively) that was not significant (two-way ANOVA: F[134] = 0.98, p = 0.3).
source: To test whether CF timing can provide a code for stimulus strength under conditions of constant stimulus duration, we varied the pressure of the airpuff. This led to a modest reduction in onset latency (81.3 ± 2.4 vs 79.6 ± 3.4 ms for p1 and p2 respectively) that was not significant (Figure 4D–F left; two-way ANOVA: F[134] = 0.98, p = 0.3), and did not alter temporal jitter (Figure 4F right; two-way ANOVA: F[134] = 0.13, p = 0.7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Varying airpuff pressure did not alter temporal jitter (two-way ANOVA: F[134] = 0.13, p = 0.7).
source: To test whether CF timing can provide a code for stimulus strength under conditions of constant stimulus duration, we varied the pressure of the airpuff. This led to a modest reduction in onset latency (81.3 ± 2.4 vs 79.6 ± 3.4 ms for p1 and p2 respectively) that was not significant (Figure 4D–F left; two-way ANOVA: F[134] = 0.98, p = 0.3), and did not alter temporal jitter (Figure 4F right; two-way ANOVA: F[134] = 0.13, p = 0.7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Higher-pressure airpuffs evoked more calcium events throughout the analysis window, both in the 0–75 ms interval (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p < 0.01) and in the 75–150 ms interval (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p < 0.001).
source: Higher-pressure airpuffs evoked more calcium events throughout the analysis window, both in the 0–75 ms interval (Figure 4E; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p < 0.01), and in the 75–150 ms interval (Figure 4E; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The onset latency of an individual climbing fiber input cannot be used to encode the pressure of the airpuff.
source: These findings indicate that the onset latency of an individual CF input cannot be used to encode the pressure of the airpuff.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing no significant latency differences with pressure changes.

claim: Groups of climbing fibers converging on the same zone of cerebellar cortex become synchronized in response to sensory stimulation.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that groups of CFs converging on the same zone of cerebellar cortex become synchronized in response to sensory stimulation (Lou and Bloedel, 1992; Ozden et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2009; Wise et al., 2010; Ghosh et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The number of synchronized calcium events in a 150 ms window after stimulus onset increased in response to airpuffs of longer durations (two-way ANOVA, F[4394] = 199.75, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.05 for all pairwise comparisons).
source: In 16 experiments in which we were able to image at least six PC dendrites simultaneously (Figure 5), we found that the number of synchronized calcium events in a 150 ms window after stimulus onset increased in response to airpuffs of longer durations (Figure 5A,B, top: two-way ANOVA, F[4394] = 199.75, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.05 for all pairwise comparisons), and higher pressures (Figure 5B, bottom: two-way ANOVA, F[2209] = 106.56, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The number of synchronized calcium events in a 150 ms window after stimulus onset increased in response to airpuffs of higher pressures (two-way ANOVA, F[2209] = 106.56, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons).
source: In 16 experiments in which we were able to image at least six PC dendrites simultaneously (Figure 5), we found that the number of synchronized calcium events in a 150 ms window after stimulus onset increased in response to airpuffs of longer durations (Figure 5A,B, top: two-way ANOVA, F[4394] = 199.75, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.05 for all pairwise comparisons), and higher pressures (Figure 5B, bottom: two-way ANOVA, F[2209] = 106.56, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Joint probability deviated significantly from the independence assumption for all airpuff strengths (two sample t test, p < 0.001).
source: We found that joint probability deviated significantly from the independence assumption for all airpuff strengths (Figure 5C; two sample t test, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was a gradual boost in the amount of extra synchrony as the airpuff duration was increased (Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[4361] = 113.49, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001, except for d3–d4 comparison).
source: Figure 5D shows that there was a gradual boost in the amount of extra synchrony as the airpuff duration or pressure was increased (Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[4361] = 113.49, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001, except for d3–d4 comparison. Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[2136] = 10.27, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05, except for p1–p2 comparison).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was a gradual boost in the amount of extra synchrony as the airpuff pressure was increased (Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[2136] = 10.27, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05, except for p1–p2 comparison).
source: Figure 5D shows that there was a gradual boost in the amount of extra synchrony as the airpuff duration or pressure was increased (Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[4361] = 113.49, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001, except for d3–d4 comparison. Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[2136] = 10.27, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05, except for p1–p2 comparison).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The degree to which climbing fibers are dependent on each other scales up smoothly with their overall response probability.
source: In other words, the degree to which CFs are dependent on each other scales up smoothly with their overall response probability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the extra synchrony analysis.

claim: Climbing fiber co-activation may be controlled upstream, perhaps in the inferior olive, in a way that provides information about stimulus strength at the level of the Purkinje cell population.
source: These results suggest that CF co-activation may be controlled upstream, perhaps in the inferior olive, in a way that provides information about stimulus strength at the level of the PC population.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The amplitude of climbing fiber-triggered calcium events is enhanced during sensory stimulation.
source: We have recently shown that the amplitude of CF-triggered calcium events is enhanced during sensory stimulation (Najafi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Periocular airpuffs of longer duration evoked progressively larger calcium events (Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 80.74, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d2–d3 comparison).
source: This analysis confirmed that periocular airpuffs of longer duration and higher pressure evoked progressively larger calcium events (Figure 6A, bottom; Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 80.74, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d2–d3 comparison. Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 62.88, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.01 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Periocular airpuffs of higher pressure evoked progressively larger calcium events (Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 62.88, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.01 for all pairwise comparisons).
source: This analysis confirmed that periocular airpuffs of longer duration and higher pressure evoked progressively larger calcium events (Figure 6A, bottom; Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 80.74, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d2–d3 comparison. Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 62.88, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.01 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The calcium elevation evoked in Purkinje cell dendrite after activation of its climbing fiber input provides information about the strength of peripheral stimulation.
source: Thus, the calcium elevation evoked in PC dendrite after activation of its CF input provides information about the strength of peripheral stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on calcium event amplitudes.

claim: Sensory stimulation elicits a smaller calcium response that has a non-climbing fiber origin ('non-CF signal').
source: In addition to triggering calcium events in the PC dendrite, sensory stimulation also elicits a smaller calcium response that has a non-CF origin ('non-CF signal'; [Najafi et al., 2014]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The rise time of the non-CF signal increased with airpuff duration (73 ± 8, 114 ± 7, 130 ± 7, 148 ± 7 ms for d1–d4 respectively; two-way ANOVA: F[375] = 12, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d2–d3 comparison).
source: We found that the rise time (73 ± 8, 114 ± 7, 130 ± 7, 148 ± 7 ms for d1–d4 respectively; two-way ANOVA: F[375] = 12, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d2–d3 comparison) and the size of this non-CF signal were graded (Figure 6B, top), with ΔF/F-integral becoming progressively larger as the stimulus duration or pressure was increased (Figure 6B bottom; Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 122.61, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001, except for d3–d4 comparison. Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 71.85, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The size of the non-CF signal became progressively larger as the stimulus duration was increased (Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 122.61, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001, except for d3–d4 comparison).
source: We found that the rise time (73 ± 8, 114 ± 7, 130 ± 7, 148 ± 7 ms for d1–d4 respectively; two-way ANOVA: F[375] = 12, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d2–d3 comparison) and the size of this non-CF signal were graded (Figure 6B, top), with ΔF/F-integral becoming progressively larger as the stimulus duration or pressure was increased (Figure 6B bottom; Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 122.61, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001, except for d3–d4 comparison. Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 71.85, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The size of the non-CF signal became progressively larger as the stimulus pressure was increased (Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 71.85, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons).
source: We found that the rise time (73 ± 8, 114 ± 7, 130 ± 7, 148 ± 7 ms for d1–d4 respectively; two-way ANOVA: F[375] = 12, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.05 except for d2–d3 comparison) and the size of this non-CF signal were graded (Figure 6B, top), with ΔF/F-integral becoming progressively larger as the stimulus duration or pressure was increased (Figure 6B bottom; Duration data: two-way ANOVA: F[496] = 122.61, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001, except for d3–d4 comparison. Pressure data: two-way ANOVA: F[238] = 71.85, p < 0.0001; Tukey's HSD: p < 0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The properties of the non-CF signal are consistent with calcium responses driven by activation of parallel fiber inputs to Purkinje cells.
source: These properties are consistent with the calcium responses driven by activation of parallel fiber inputs to PCs (Finch and Augustine, 1998; Takechi et al., 1998) which are known to increase progressively with stimulus duration (Gandolfi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited previous studies of parallel fiber responses.

claim: For short-duration airpuffs, the average non-CF signal resembled the average enhancement trace of calcium events.
source: For short-duration airpuffs (Figure 6C, d1 and d2), the average non-CF signal resembled the average enhancement trace.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of traces shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For the longest-duration airpuffs, the non-CF signal was significantly smaller than the enhancement trace.
source: However, for the longest-duration airpuffs (Figure 6C, d4), the non-CF signal was significantly smaller than the enhancement trace.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of traces shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Calcium events evoked by relatively weak sensory stimulation comprise a constant climbing fiber-triggered signal that adds linearly with a non-CF signal graded according to the strength of the stimulus.
source: These results are consistent with a model in which calcium events evoked by relatively weak sensory stimulation comprise a constant CF-triggered signal that adds linearly with a non-CF signal graded according to the strength of the stimulus (Figure 6D, d1, d2, d3).
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the experimental observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The supralinear response evoked by very strong airpuffs could be explained if these stimuli were effective in triggering more spikes in each individual climbing fiber burst.
source: The supralinear response evoked by very strong airpuffs (Figure 6D, d4, arrowhead) could be explained if these stimuli were effective in triggering more spikes in each individual CF burst (Maruta et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the supralinear response, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Climbing fibers represent information about the strength of a periocular airpuff in a number of ways, both at the individual-CF and population level.
source: Our results demonstrate that climbing fibers (CFs) represent information about the strength of a periocular airpuff in a number of ways, both at the individual-CF and population level.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Each presentation of the periocular airpuff resulted in either zero or one calcium event in the Purkinje cell dendrite (multiple activation in <2% of all trials).
source: Consistent with previous reports of CF activity in awake animals (Gibson et al., 2004), we found no evidence for rate coding in our experiments: each presentation of the periocular airpuff resulted in either zero or one calcium event in the Purkinje cell (PC) dendrite, which would indicate that the pre-synaptic CF was activated at most once in virtually all trials (multiple activation in <2% of all trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citation to previous work.

claim: There is no evidence for rate coding in climbing fiber responses to periocular airpuffs.
source: Consistent with previous reports of CF activity in awake animals (Gibson et al., 2004), we found no evidence for rate coding in our experiments: each presentation of the periocular airpuff resulted in either zero or one calcium event in the Purkinje cell (PC) dendrite, which would indicate that the pre-synaptic CF was activated at most once in virtually all trials (multiple activation in <2% of all trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citation to previous work.

claim: Every time the climbing fiber input fires, it triggers a wide range of synaptic changes in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Every time the CF input fires, it triggers a wide range of synaptic changes in the cerebellar cortex (Schmolesky et al., 2002; Ohtsuki et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies of CF-induced plasticity.

claim: The total amount of plasticity induced in the cerebellar cortex during training is likely to depend on the reliability with which climbing fibers are activated by repeated presentations of the instructive stimulus.
source: Thus, the total amount of plasticity induced in the cerebellar cortex during training is likely to depend on the reliability with which CFs are activated by the repeated presentations of the instructive stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and knowledge of CF-induced plasticity.

claim: Plasticity in Purkinje cells is strongly influenced by the relative timing of synaptic inputs.
source: As is the case for neurons other brain regions (Dan and Poo, 2004), plasticity in PCs is strongly influenced by the relative timing of synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

claim: Parallel fiber synapses activated just before the climbing fiber input get weaker.
source: For example, parallel fiber (PF) synapses activated just before the CF input get weaker, whereas those activated just after the CF input get stronger (Piochon et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous plasticity studies.

claim: Parallel fiber synapses activated just after the climbing fiber input get stronger.
source: For example, parallel fiber (PF) synapses activated just before the CF input get weaker, whereas those activated just after the CF input get stronger (Piochon et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous plasticity studies.

claim: The total amount of plasticity induced in a Purkinje cell over the course of multiple training trials will vary as a function of the number of times the instructive stimulus is able to activate the climbing fiber within the same small window of time.
source: Therefore, we predict that the total amount of plasticity induced in a PC over the course of multiple training trials will vary as a function of the number of times the instructive stimulus is able to activate the CF within the same small window of time.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings about CF timing and knowledge of timing-dependent plasticity.

claim: Parallel fiber and climbing fiber inputs with similar receptive fields often converge on the same Purkinje cell.
source: Although the source of the non-CF signal is unknown, we note that the excitatory parallel fiber (PF) input satisfies two conditions necessary to play such a role: (1) PF and CF inputs with similar receptive fields often converge on the same PC (Eccles et al., 1972a; Eccles, 1973), and (2) stimulation of PFs generates graded calcium responses in PC dendrites (Eilers et al., 1995; Gandolfi et al., 2014), that have similar kinetics to the non-CF signal (Finch and Augustine, 1998; Takechi et al., 1998; Wang et al., 2000) and can boost the amplitude of CF-triggered dendritic calcium events (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Stimulation of parallel fibers generates graded calcium responses in Purkinje cell dendrites.
source: Although the source of the non-CF signal is unknown, we note that the excitatory parallel fiber (PF) input satisfies two conditions necessary to play such a role: (1) PF and CF inputs with similar receptive fields often converge on the same PC (Eccles et al., 1972a; Eccles, 1973), and (2) stimulation of PFs generates graded calcium responses in PC dendrites (Eilers et al., 1995; Gandolfi et al., 2014), that have similar kinetics to the non-CF signal (Finch and Augustine, 1998; Takechi et al., 1998; Wang et al., 2000) and can boost the amplitude of CF-triggered dendritic calcium events (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous calcium imaging studies.

claim: Parallel fiber-evoked calcium responses can boost the amplitude of climbing fiber-triggered dendritic calcium events.
source: Although the source of the non-CF signal is unknown, we note that the excitatory parallel fiber (PF) input satisfies two conditions necessary to play such a role: (1) PF and CF inputs with similar receptive fields often converge on the same PC (Eccles et al., 1972a; Eccles, 1973), and (2) stimulation of PFs generates graded calcium responses in PC dendrites (Eilers et al., 1995; Gandolfi et al., 2014), that have similar kinetics to the non-CF signal (Finch and Augustine, 1998; Takechi et al., 1998; Wang et al., 2000) and can boost the amplitude of CF-triggered dendritic calcium events (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The number of spikes in the presynaptic climbing fiber burst varies systematically depending on experimental conditions both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Recent studies have shown that the number of spikes in the presynaptic CF burst varies systematically depending on experimental conditions both in vitro (Mathy et al., 2009) and in vivo (Maruta et al., 2007; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012), and that having just one extra spike in the CF burst can cause a substantial enhancement of the postsynaptic calcium response (Mathy et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological and imaging studies.

claim: Having just one extra spike in the climbing fiber burst can cause a substantial enhancement of the postsynaptic calcium response.
source: Recent studies have shown that the number of spikes in the presynaptic CF burst varies systematically depending on experimental conditions both in vitro (Mathy et al., 2009) and in vivo (Maruta et al., 2007; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012), and that having just one extra spike in the CF burst can cause a substantial enhancement of the postsynaptic calcium response (Mathy et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The graded modulation of calcium events could be driven in part by small increases in the number of spikes of the climbing fiber burst, especially for the longest stimulus durations.
source: These observations raise the possibility that the graded modulation of calcium events in our experiments could be driven in part by small increases in the number of spikes of the CF burst (Najafi and Medina, 2013; Yang and Lisberger, 2014), especially for the longest stimulus durations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citations.

claim: Dendritic calcium is responsible for triggering a variety of mechanisms of cellular plasticity that cause short- and long-term modifications in the strength of Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Dendritic calcium is responsible for triggering a variety of mechanisms of cellular plasticity that cause short- and long-term modifications in the strength of PC synapses (Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of cerebellar plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Plasticity mechanisms in Purkinje cells are tightly regulated and can be differentially engaged depending on the precise amplitude and duration of the calcium signal in the dendrite.
source: These plasticity mechanisms are tightly regulated and can be differentially engaged depending on the precise amplitude and duration of the calcium signal in the PC dendrite.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of calcium-dependent plasticity.

claim: Small differences in dendritic calcium can influence how much parallel fiber synapses will change in vitro.
source: For example, small differences in dendritic calcium can influence how much PF synapses will change in vitro (Coesmans et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2007), and can also determine the direction of learning-related changes in the firing of PCs recorded in vivo during eyeblink conditioning (Rasmussen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous plasticity studies.

claim: Small differences in dendritic calcium can determine the direction of learning-related changes in the firing of Purkinje cells recorded in vivo during eyeblink conditioning.
source: For example, small differences in dendritic calcium can influence how much PF synapses will change in vitro (Coesmans et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2007), and can also determine the direction of learning-related changes in the firing of PCs recorded in vivo during eyeblink conditioning (Rasmussen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous in vivo studies.

claim: The amount and direction of plasticity induced in a Purkinje cell during cerebellar learning will vary trial-by-trial depending on the dendritic calcium response triggered by each presentation of the instructive stimulus.
source: Thus, we predict that the amount and direction of plasticity induced in a PC during cerebellar learning will vary trial-by-trial depending on the dendritic calcium response triggered by each presentation of the instructive stimulus.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings and knowledge of calcium-dependent plasticity.

claim: Trial-by-trial regulation of climbing fiber-related instructive signals has been demonstrated in monkeys learning a cerebellar-dependent eye movement task.
source: This type of trial-by-trial regulation of CF-related instructive signals has been recently demonstrated in monkeys learning a cerebellar-dependent eye movement task (Yang and Lisberger, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent work in primates.

claim: Climbing fibers converging on the same parasagittal strip of cerebellar cortex fire synchronously to signal the occurrence of an unexpected stimulus.
source: Previous studies have reported that CFs converging on the same parasagittal strip of cerebellar cortex fire synchronously to signal the occurrence of an unexpected stimulus (Llinás and Sasaki, 1989; Lou and Bloedel, 1992; Ozden et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2009; Wise et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The level of climbing fiber synchronization is regulated by the strength of the stimulus.
source: Our results confirm and extend these findings in two ways: First, we demonstrated that the level of synchronization is regulated by the strength of the stimulus, that is a larger fraction of the local CF population was activated after strong periocular airpuffs than after weak airpuffs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data on CF co-activation.

claim: Stimulus-related differences in the level of synchronization are partly driven by a mechanism that boosts synchrony beyond what is expected for independent climbing fibers.
source: Second, we found that stimulus-related differences in the level of synchronization are partly driven by a mechanism that boosts synchrony beyond what is expected for independent CFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental analysis of extra synchrony.

claim: Electrical coupling of cells in the inferior olive plays an important role in synchronizing climbing fiber activity.
source: However, we note that electrical coupling of cells in the inferior olive (IO) plays an important role in synchronizing CF activity (De Zeeuw et al., 1997; Blenkinsop and Lang, 2006; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008), and that the coupling coefficient can be dynamically modulated up and down via stimulus-related activation of synaptic inputs to the IO (Llinás and Sasaki, 1989; Lang, 2002; Lefler et al., 2014; De Gruijl et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies of inferior olive physiology.

claim: The coupling coefficient in the inferior olive can be dynamically modulated up and down via stimulus-related activation of synaptic inputs.
source: However, we note that electrical coupling of cells in the inferior olive (IO) plays an important role in synchronizing CF activity (De Zeeuw et al., 1997; Blenkinsop and Lang, 2006; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008), and that the coupling coefficient can be dynamically modulated up and down via stimulus-related activation of synaptic inputs to the IO (Llinás and Sasaki, 1989; Lang, 2002; Lefler et al., 2014; De Gruijl et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Regulation of climbing fiber synchrony could be used to control the efficacy of plasticity signals.
source: Regulation of CF synchrony could be used to control the efficacy of plasticity signals (De Gruijl et al., 2012; Tokuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Sensory events that activate many climbing fibers simultaneously may be particularly effective for triggering NMDA-dependent plasticity in molecular layer interneurons of the cerebellar cortex.
source: For example, sensory events that activate many CFs simultaneously may be particularly effective for triggering NMDA-dependent plasticity in molecular layer interneurons of the cerebellar cortex (Duguid and Smart, 2004), via synchronized spillover of glutamate from multiple CF release sites (Szapiro and Barbour, 2007; Mathews et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Climbing fiber synchrony could be used to set the strength of the plasticity signals sent by inhibitory Purkinje cells to downstream cells of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: Another possibility is that CF synchrony could be used to set the strength of the plasticity signals sent by inhibitory PCs to downstream cells of the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN; Otis et al., 2012), which are the final output of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Deep cerebellar nuclei cells exhibit rebound firing immediately after being released from the hyperpolarization caused by climbing fiber-driven synchronization of the Purkinje cell population.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with recent work showing that DCN cells exhibit rebound firing immediately after being released from the hyperpolarization caused by CF-driven synchronization of the PC population (Hoebeek et al., 2010; Bengtsson et al., 2011), and that this rebound can serve as a trigger for plasticity (Pugh and Raman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: Rebound firing in deep cerebellar nuclei cells can serve as a trigger for plasticity.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with recent work showing that DCN cells exhibit rebound firing immediately after being released from the hyperpolarization caused by CF-driven synchronization of the PC population (Hoebeek et al., 2010; Bengtsson et al., 2011), and that this rebound can serve as a trigger for plasticity (Pugh and Raman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Release from hyperpolarization may be sufficient to trigger calcium-based excitable events in dendrites of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: Release from hyperpolarization may also be sufficient to trigger calcium-based excitable events in dendrites of the DCN (Schneider et al., 2013), an effect that may be enhanced by direct monosynaptic excitation of DCN neurons by CF collaterals firing at the same time (Llinás and Muhlethaler, 1988).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Sensory-driven regulation of climbing fiber synchrony could have a direct and immediate effect on motor control.
source: In addition to playing a role in the modulation of plasticity signals in the cerebellum, sensory-driven regulation of CF synchrony could also have a more direct and immediate effect on motor control (Lang et al., 1999; Kitazawa and Wolpert, 2005; Llinás, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Increased climbing fiber synchrony is observed at the onset of movement.
source: Increased CF synchrony is observed at the onset of movement (Welsh et al., 1995; Ghosh et al., 2011; Ozden et al., 2012), and the level of synchrony has been shown to correlate with the timing and the velocity of spinocerebellar reflexes after sensory perturbations (De Gruijl et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The level of climbing fiber synchrony correlates with the timing and velocity of spinocerebellar reflexes after sensory perturbations.
source: Increased CF synchrony is observed at the onset of movement (Welsh et al., 1995; Ghosh et al., 2011; Ozden et al., 2012), and the level of synchrony has been shown to correlate with the timing and the velocity of spinocerebellar reflexes after sensory perturbations (De Gruijl et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A higher level of climbing fiber synchrony after a strong periocular airpuff might serve to enhance the reflex response by generating a faster or longer duration eyeblink movement.
source: In our experiments, a higher level of CF synchrony after a strong periocular airpuff might serve to enhance the reflex response by generating a faster or longer duration eyeblink movement (Evinger et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citation.

claim: Climbing fibers must provide analog information to indicate how unexpected an event was, that is, how much stronger or weaker the airpuff was compared with expectations.
source: To be useful, CFs must do more than alert about the occurrence of an unexpected event such as the presentation of a periocular airpuff in the early stages of eyeblink conditioning (Sears and Steinmetz, 1991; Nicholson and Freeman, 2003); they must also provide analog information to indicate how unexpected the event was, that is, how much stronger or weaker the airpuff was compared with expectations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional requirements of teaching signals.

claim: The experiments demonstrate that climbing fibers and non-CF pathways together encode information about stimulus strength in Purkinje cell dendrites when the presentation of the stimulus cannot be predicted.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that CFs and non-CF pathways together encode information about stimulus strength in PC dendrites when the presentation of the stimulus cannot be predicted.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.
